title: Two Sum on sorted array — left+right pointer, O(1) space.
shortTitle: Two Sum on a Sorted Array — Left and Right Pointers, O(1) Space

s1_definition.profdef: Two Sum on a sorted array finds two elements whose values add up to a given target using opposite-end two pointers. A `left` pointer starts at the smallest value and a `right` pointer at the largest; based on whether their sum is below or above the target you move one pointer inward. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, improving on the hash-map version which needs O(n) memory.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has a sorted list of past deposit amounts and wants to know which two deposits together equal a disputed figure. He puts one finger on the smallest deposit and one on the largest. If their total is too small he slides the low finger up to a bigger deposit; if too big he slides the high finger down. He finds the pair without scribbling a side list of everything he has seen.
s1_definition.oneliner: On sorted data, two opposite-end pointers find a target pair in one linear pass with zero extra memory.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two Sum on a sorted array finds two elements whose values add up to a given target using opposite-end two pointers. A `left` pointer starts at the smallest value and a `right` pointer at the largest; based on whether their sum is below or above the target you move one pointer inward. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, improving on the hash-map version which needs O(n) memory.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh has a sorted list of past deposit amounts and wants to know which two deposits together equal a disputed figure. He puts one finger on the smallest deposit and one on the largest. If their total is too small he slides the low finger up to a bigger deposit; if too big he slides the high finger down. He finds the pair without scribbling a side list of everything he has seen.

**One line to remember:** On sorted data, two opposite-end pointers find a target pair in one linear pass with zero extra memory.

sections.s2_technical:
The method keeps two indexes, `left` at index 0 and `right` at the last index. The loop condition is `while (left < right)`. Inside, you compute `sum = a[left] + a[right]`. Three cases follow. If `sum == target` you found the answer and return the indexes or the values. If `sum < target` the only way to increase the sum is to move `left` up to a larger value, so `left++`. If `sum > target` you must decrease the sum, so `right--`.

Why does moving a single pointer never miss a valid pair? Because the array is sorted, when `sum < target` the value at `left` is too small even when paired with the largest remaining value at `right`, so `left` can never be part of the answer and is safely discarded. The symmetric argument holds when `sum > target`. This is the key correctness insight interviewers probe.

A code snippet for banking amounts: `int[] twoSum(int[] amounts, int target) { int l = 0, r = amounts.length - 1; while (l < r) { int s = amounts[l] + amounts[r]; if (s == target) return new int[]{l, r}; if (s < target) l++; else r--; } return new int[]{-1, -1}; }`. Each iteration moves at least one pointer, and they never cross back, so total work is linear.

A senior nuance is the precondition: the array must be sorted, and many interviewers hand you the classic LeetCode variant where indexes are one-based. If the input is unsorted and you cannot change ordering, the hash-map approach is correct instead because sorting would destroy original indexes unless you keep a mapping. Also watch for integer overflow on very large amounts, for which you would use `long` or `BigDecimal` in real money code.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India reconciliation desk sees a disputed charge and suspects it is the sum of two legitimate debits that were double-counted. The debits are already stored sorted by amount. They must find whether two of them add up to the disputed amount. This is exactly how sorted Two Sum works — opposite-end pointers close in on the pair without extra memory.

Problem 2 — Because real money cannot use int, the service works in paise-as-long internally and reports BigDecimal rupees so there is no rounding error. The pointer logic is identical; only the number type is wider.

The code shows a `ReconciliationService` with a `findMatchingPair` method using long paise, a small demo on Rajesh's sorted debit list, and a success and a failure case.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: sorted debits in paise [10000, 25000, 40000, 65000, 90000], target 65000 paise (650 rupees).

Step 1: `left` is index 0 (10000) and `right` is index 4 (90000). The sum is 100000, bigger than 65000, so `right` drops to index 3 (65000). The array is untouched; only `right` changed.

Step 2: Sum is 10000 plus 65000 equals 75000, still bigger, so `right` drops to index 2 (40000). Sum is 10000 plus 40000 equals 50000, now smaller than 65000, so `left` rises to index 1 (25000).

Step 3: Sum is 25000 plus 40000 equals 65000, which matches, so we return indexes [1, 2]. Converting back to rupees gives 250.00 plus 400.00 equals 650.00.

Step 4: For the second call with target 1 paise, the smallest possible sum is 10000 plus 25000 which is already far above 1, so `right` keeps dropping until `left` meets `right` and the loop ends with no match, returning [-1, -1].

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Match at indexes 1,2
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Pair indexes for 650.00: [1, 2] = 250.00 + 400.00
2026-10-26 21:00:03 WARNING No pair sums to target 1 paise
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Pair indexes for 0.01: [-1, -1]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Two Sum on a sorted array finds two values that add up to a target using opposite-end two pointers, giving linear time and constant extra space. I place a left pointer on the smallest value and a right pointer on the largest. If their sum is less than the target I move the left pointer up to a larger value, if the sum is greater than the target I move the right pointer down to a smaller value, and if the sum equals the target I return the pair. Each pointer only moves inward and they never cross back, so the whole array is scanned once.

The correctness argument is the part interviewers want to hear. Because the array is sorted, when the current sum is too small the smallest value can never contribute to a valid pair even alongside the largest remaining value, so I can safely discard it by advancing the left pointer, and the mirror image holds when the sum is too large. That reasoning is why moving one pointer at a time never skips the answer.

The trade-off against the hash-map version is memory. The hash-map approach works on unsorted data in linear time but needs linear extra space to remember what it has seen, while the sorted two-pointer approach needs no extra space but requires the input to already be sorted. I pick based on whether the data is sorted and whether memory is tight.

In my banking work at the National Bank of India I used this in the reconciliation service to decide whether a disputed charge was the sum of two legitimate debits that had been double-counted, working in long paise internally to avoid overflow and reporting BigDecimal rupees so there was never a rounding error. Explaining the pointer movement, the correctness reasoning, the space trade-off, and the money-type caution shows the interviewer I understand both the algorithm and its real constraints.
